newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Syrian troop movements give Israel war jitters.
newsitem.headline: Syrian troop movements give Israel war jitters.

text.p: Syria has given Israel its worst case of war jitters since the bitter enemies began unfruitful peace talks five years ago.

While world attention has been focused on U.S.-Iraqi tension Syrian President Hafez al-Assad has redeployed up to 12,000 troops in Lebanon, moving some within striking distance of a key Israeli position on the Golan Heights.
Israeli commentators said on Tuesday he was sending a clear message to the right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu: Talk peace seriously or risk the prospect of war.
"They are preparing an infrastructure for a military option, if their signals do not bear fruit and if the diplomatic process gets stuck," military analyst Ron Ben-Yishai told Army Radio.

Unlike the previous Labour-led government, Netanyahu opposes trading occupied Arab land for peace and says the Golan Heights, which Israel captured from Syria in the 1967 Middle East, must remain under Israeli sovereignty.
Before it returns to peace talks broken off by Israel after Moslem suicide bombings in February and March, Syria wants an Israeli commitment to return all the strategic plateau.
Netanyahu and the United States have been trying to come up with a formula to restart the negotiations. U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross was due back in the region on Tuesday.
The prime minister and his defence chief, Yitzhak Mordechai, assured Israelis on Monday there was no cause for concern but said events in the north were being closely monitored.
None of Israel's top military analysts or leaders predicted any immediate outbreak of hostilities.

"I think it is hard for us to understand why this redeployment has taken place," said Internal Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani. "It appears to me that it is partly aimed at getting the diplomatic process moving."

But Assad's decision to shift the troops -- a redeployment undertaken after Netanyahu visited south Lebanon last month and said Hizbollah guerrilla attacks against Israeli soldiers were "not good for Syria" -- put war on the public agenda in Israel.

"This movement of forces and tension that has continued already for more than two weeks are the first such developments since (the 1991 Madrid Middle East peace conference)," said Itamar Rabinovich, Israel's former chief negotiator with Syria.
Israeli newspaper headlines, which have focused on tensions with Syria for days, spoke of intensive U.S. efforts to avoid brinkmanship.

Netanyahu issued a rare invitation to the man he defeated in last May's elections, former Prime Minister Shimon Peres, to meet him later on Tuesday. Israel Radio said they would discuss the Syrian crisis and other issues.
A spokesman for Netanyahu declined to comment on a report in the Maariv newspaper that Assad had sent a "threatening message" to Israel via U.S. Ambassador Martin Indyk.
Newspapers carried maps showing new Syrian positions, a day after Mordechai briefed Israeli military correspondents on the situation.
If Assad is waging psychological warfare, he has managed to push all the right buttons.
According to the Israeli reports, Syria moved its troops near scenes of past battles with Israel that left deep scars in the Jewish state.

A brigade from its 10th Mechanised Division moved from north of Beirut to the Bekaa Valley, near the site of an Israeli-Syrian tank battle during Israel's 1982 invasion of Lebanon, the reports said. Three Israeli soldiers are still listed as missing from that battle.

The reports also said special forces from Syria's 14th Division redeployed from Beirut to an area east of Mount Hermon. Syrian commandos captured Israel's outpost on the mountain at the start of the 1973 Middle East war. In subsequent fighting, Israel retook it at a heavy cost.
And fears that Syria might be planning an attack to break the peace stalemate coincided with the approach of the Yom Kippur fast day next Monday.

Many Israelis' worst nightmare is the 1973 Syrian and Egyptian surprise attacks on the Jewish Day of Atonement, when reservists in prayer shawls were called out of synagogues and air raid sirens wailed.

"I think the people have to continue to celebrate its holidays and to be prepared for Yom Kippur, not the one for Yom Kippur 1973 but one where we can go to synagogue in peace," said Kahalani, who commanded Israeli tanks on the Golan 23 years ago.
